units.meaning: 29 CFR 825.110 provides regulations defining and governing 'Eligible employee' under the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA), serving as a descriptive section heading without independent operative requirements.

An 'eligible employee' under the FMLA is defined as an employee of a covered employer who simultaneously satisfies three criteria: (1) has been employed by the employer for at least 12 months; (2) has been employed for at least 1,250 hours of service during the 12-month period immediately preceding the commencement of the leave (subject to special rules for airline flight crew employees in § 825.801); and (3) is employed at a worksite where 50 or more employees are employed by the employer within 75 miles of that worksite (referencing § 825.105(b) for employees working outside the U.S.).

The 12 months that an employee must have been employed by the employer to meet the FMLA eligibility requirement do not need to be consecutive months, subject to the conditions and break-in-service rules set forth in paragraph (b).

Subject to the exceptions specified in paragraph (b)(2), employment periods prior to a break in service of seven years or more are not required to be counted when determining whether an employee has been employed by the employer for at least 12 months.

Employment periods preceding a break in service of more than seven years must be counted toward the 12-month employment requirement if the employee's break in service is occasioned by the fulfillment of a Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act (USERRA) covered service obligation. Furthermore, the period of absence from work due to or necessitated by USERRA-covered service must also be counted in determining whether the employee has been employed for at least 12 months, although this section provides no greater entitlement than available under USERRA.

Employment periods preceding a break in service of more than seven years must be counted toward the 12-month employment requirement where a written agreement, including a collective bargaining agreement, exists concerning the employer's intention to rehire the employee after the break in service (such as for the purpose of furthering education or childrearing).

If an employee is maintained on the payroll for any part of a week—including any periods of paid or unpaid leave (such as sick leave or vacation) during which other benefits or compensation (e.g., workers' compensation, group health plan benefits) are provided by the employer—that week counts as a week of employment. For determining whether intermittent, occasional, or casual employment qualifies as at least 12 months, 52 weeks is deemed equal to 12 months.

Employers are permitted to consider an employee's employment prior to a continuous break in service of more than seven years when determining whether the employee has met the 12-month employment requirement, even when not mandated to do so.

If an employer chooses to recognize prior employment before a continuous break in service of more than seven years, the employer must do so uniformly with respect to all employees with similar breaks in service.

Except as provided in paragraph (c)(2) and § 825.801 for airline flight crew employees, whether an employee has worked the minimum 1,250 hours of service during the 12-month period is determined according to Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) principles for determining compensable hours of work (29 CFR part 785). The determining factor is the actual number of hours worked within the meaning of the FLSA; the determination is not limited by methods of recordkeeping or inaccurate compensation agreements, and any accurate accounting of actual hours worked under FLSA principles may be used.

An employee returning from USERRA-covered service must be credited with the hours of service that would have been performed but for the period of absence from work due to or necessitated by USERRA-covered service when determining eligibility for FMLA-qualifying leave, adding those hours to hours actually worked during the previous 12-month period. To calculate the hours that would have been worked during that absence, the employee's pre-service work schedule can generally be used (with special rules in § 825.801(c) for airline flight crew employees).

If an employer does not maintain an accurate record of hours worked by an employee—including employees exempt from FLSA recordkeeping requirements, such as bona fide executive, administrative, and professional employees—the employer bears the burden of showing that the employee has not worked the requisite 1,250 hours. To claim such employees (e.g., full-time teachers who often work outside the classroom or at home) are ineligible for FMLA leave, the employer must be able to clearly demonstrate that the employee did not work 1,250 hours during the previous 12 months (subject to § 825.801(d) for airline flight crew employees).
The determination of whether an employee meets the 1,250 hours of service requirement and has been employed for at least 12 months must be made as of the date the FMLA leave is to start.

An employee may be on non-FMLA leave at the time the 12-month eligibility requirement is met; in that event, any portion of the leave taken for an FMLA-qualifying reason after meeting the eligibility requirement is treated as FMLA leave.
Whether 50 employees are employed within 75 miles of the worksite to establish FMLA eligibility is determined at the time the employee gives notice of the need for leave.

Once an employee is determined eligible in response to a notice of need for leave (whether taken all at once, intermittently, or on a reduced schedule), the employee's eligibility for that specific notice cannot be affected by any subsequent change in employee headcount at or within 75 miles of the worksite, and the employer is prohibited from terminating leave that has already started if the employee count drops below 50 (e.g., notice in August when 60 employees are employed requires granting leave starting in December even if headcount drops to 40).

units.meaning: Section heading designating 29 CFR 825.110 regarding eligible employees, containing no independent operative requirements or rights.
An eligible employee is an employee of a covered employer who has been employed by the employer for at least 12 months.

To be an eligible employee, the employee must have been employed for at least 1,250 hours of service during the 12-month period immediately preceding the commencement of the leave (subject to special rules in § 825.801 for airline flight crew employees).

To be an eligible employee, the employee must be employed at a worksite where 50 or more employees are employed by the employer within 75 miles of that worksite (referencing § 825.105(b) regarding employees who work outside the U.S.).
The 12 months an employee must have been employed by the employer need not be consecutive months, subject to the conditions in paragraph (b).

Subject to the exceptions in paragraph (b)(2), employment periods prior to a break in service of seven years or more need not be counted when determining whether the employee has been employed by the employer for at least 12 months.

Employment periods preceding a break in service of more than seven years must be counted in determining whether an employee has been employed for at least 12 months where the employee's break in service is occasioned by fulfilling a USERRA-covered service obligation, and the period of absence due to or necessitated by USERRA-covered service must also be counted, provided this section gives no greater entitlement than available under USERRA.

Employment periods preceding a break in service of more than seven years must be counted in determining whether an employee has been employed for at least 12 months where a written agreement, including a collective bargaining agreement, exists concerning the employer's intention to rehire the employee after the break in service (such as for education or childrearing purposes).

If an employee is maintained on the payroll for any part of a week, including periods of paid or unpaid leave (sick, vacation) during which other benefits or compensation are provided by the employer (such as workers' compensation or group health plan benefits), that week counts as a week of employment.
For the purpose of determining whether intermittent, occasional, or casual employment qualifies as at least 12 months, 52 weeks is deemed equal to 12 months.

Employers are not prevented from considering employment prior to a continuous break in service of more than seven years when determining whether an employee has met the 12-month employment requirement.

If an employer chooses to recognize prior employment before a continuous break in service of more than seven years, the employer must do so uniformly with respect to all employees with similar breaks in service.

Except as provided in paragraph (c)(2) and § 825.801 for airline flight crew employees, whether an employee has worked the minimum 1,250 hours of service is determined by the number of hours worked for the employer within the meaning of compensable hours of work under FLSA principles (29 CFR part 785).
The determination of hours worked is not limited by methods of recordkeeping or inaccurate compensation agreements; any accurate accounting of actual hours worked under FLSA principles may be used.

An employee returning from USERRA-covered service must be credited with the hours of service that would have been performed but for the absence necessitated by USERRA-covered service when determining FMLA eligibility, adding those hours to hours actually worked during the previous 12-month period.

To determine the hours that would have been worked during an absence due to USERRA-covered service, the employee's pre-service work schedule can generally be used for calculations (referencing § 825.801(c) for airline flight crew employees).

If an employer does not maintain an accurate record of hours worked by an employee, including employees exempt from FLSA recordkeeping requirements (such as executive, administrative, and professional employees under 29 CFR part 541), the employer bears the burden of showing that the employee has not worked the requisite hours.

Where an employer claims that full-time teachers of an elementary or secondary school system, institution of higher education, or other educational establishment are not eligible for FMLA leave, the employer must be able to clearly demonstrate that the teachers did not work 1,250 hours during the previous 12 months (referencing § 825.801(d) for airline flight crew employees).
The determination of whether an employee meets the hours of service requirement and has been employed for a total of at least 12 months must be made as of the date the FMLA leave is to start.

An employee may be on non-FMLA leave when meeting the 12-month eligibility requirement; in that event, any portion of the leave taken for an FMLA-qualifying reason after meeting the requirement is FMLA leave (referencing § 825.300(b) for eligibility notice rules).
Whether 50 employees are employed within 75 miles to determine FMLA eligibility is determined when the employee gives notice of the need for leave.

Once an employee is determined eligible in response to a notice of the need for leave (whether taken all at once, intermittently, or on a reduced schedule), that eligibility for that specific notice is not affected by any subsequent change in the employee count within 75 miles of the worksite.
An employer may not terminate an employee's leave that has already started if the employee count drops below 50.

If an employer employs 60 employees in August but expects the count to drop to 40 in December, the employer must grant FMLA benefits to an otherwise eligible employee who gives notice in August for leave beginning in December.

units.meaning: 29 CFR 825.110 provides the title and subject heading defining and establishing the rules for an eligible employee under the Family and Medical Leave Act.

An eligible employee is defined as an employee of a covered employer who has been employed by the employer for at least 12 months, has been employed for at least 1,250 hours of service during the 12-month period immediately preceding the commencement of the leave (subject to special requirements for airline flight crew employees under 29 CFR 825.801), and is employed at a worksite where 50 or more employees are employed by the employer within 75 miles of that worksite.
The 12 months an employee must have been employed by the employer need not be consecutive months, provided the qualifying conditions regarding breaks in service are met.

Subject to the specified exceptions for USERRA service or written rehire agreements, employment periods prior to a break in service of seven years or more need not be counted in determining whether the employee has been employed by the employer for at least 12 months.

Employment periods preceding a break in service of more than seven years must be counted in determining whether the employee has been employed by the employer for at least 12 months where the employee's break in service is occasioned by the fulfillment of their USERRA-covered service obligation, and the period of absence from work due to or necessitated by USERRA-covered service must also be counted toward the 12-month requirement, provided that this section does not confer any greater entitlement than is available under USERRA.

Employment periods preceding a break in service of more than seven years must be counted in determining whether the employee has been employed by the employer for at least 12 months where a written agreement, including a collective bargaining agreement, exists concerning the employer's intention to rehire the employee after the break in service (such as for education or childrearing purposes).

If an employee is maintained on the payroll for any part of a week, including any periods of paid or unpaid leave (such as sick leave or vacation) during which other benefits or compensation are provided by the employer (e.g., workers' compensation or group health plan benefits), the week counts as a week of employment; and for intermittent, occasional, or casual employment, 52 weeks is deemed equal to 12 months.
Employers are permitted to consider employment prior to a continuous break in service of more than seven years when determining whether an employee has met the 12-month employment requirement.

If an employer chooses to recognize prior employment preceding a continuous break in service of more than seven years, the employer must do so uniformly with respect to all employees with similar breaks in service.

Except as provided for USERRA-covered service and in 29 CFR 825.801 for airline flight crew employees, whether an employee has worked the minimum 1,250 hours of service is determined according to the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) principles for compensable hours of work, based on the actual number of hours worked; this determination is not limited by methods of recordkeeping or non-reflective compensation agreements, and any accurate accounting of actual hours worked under FLSA principles may be used.

An employee reemployed following USERRA-covered service must be credited with the hours of service that would have been worked for the employer during the period of absence due to or necessitated by that service, which are added to hours actually worked during the previous 12-month period to satisfy the 1,250 hours of service requirement; the employee's pre-service work schedule can generally be used to determine those hours, subject to special rules for airline flight crew employees under 29 CFR 825.801(c).

If an employer fails to maintain an accurate record of hours worked by an employee—including employees exempt from FLSA recordkeeping requirements—the employer bears the burden of showing that the employee did not work the requisite 1,250 hours, and must be able to clearly demonstrate this fact (for example, by showing that full-time teachers did not work 1,250 hours during the previous 12 months) in order to claim the employee is ineligible for FMLA leave, subject to special rules for airline flight crew under 29 CFR 825.801(d).
The determination of whether an employee meets the hours of service requirement and the 12-month employment requirement must be made as of the date the FMLA leave is scheduled to start.

An employee may be on non-FMLA leave when they satisfy the 12-month eligibility requirement, and if so, any portion of the leave taken for an FMLA-qualifying reason after meeting the requirement constitutes FMLA leave.
Whether 50 employees are employed within 75 miles of the employee's worksite must be determined as of the date the employee gives notice of the need for leave.

Regardless of whether leave is taken at one time or on an intermittent or reduced leave schedule basis, once an employee is determined eligible based on their notice of the need for leave, their eligibility is not affected by any subsequent change in the employee headcount at or within 75 miles of the worksite for that specific notice.
An employer is prohibited from terminating an employee's leave that has already commenced if the employee headcount drops below 50.

To be an eligible employee under the FMLA, an employee of a covered employer must have been employed by the employer for at least 12 months.

To be an eligible employee under the FMLA, an employee of a covered employer must have been employed for at least 1,250 hours of service during the 12-month period immediately preceding the commencement of the leave, subject to special hours of service requirements for airline flight crew employees under 29 CFR 825.801.

To be an eligible employee under the FMLA, an employee of a covered employer must be employed at a worksite where 50 or more employees are employed by the employer within 75 miles of that worksite (referencing 29 CFR 825.105(b) regarding employees working outside the U.S.).
The 12 months of employment required for an employee to be eligible under the FMLA do not need to be consecutive months.

Subject to the exceptions in paragraph (b)(2), employment periods prior to a break in service of seven years or more do not need to be counted in determining whether an employee has been employed by the employer for at least 12 months.

Employment periods preceding a break in service of more than seven years must be counted in determining whether the employee has been employed for at least 12 months if the break in service is occasioned by the fulfillment of the employee's USERRA-covered service obligation; the period of absence from work due to or necessitated by USERRA-covered service must also be counted, though this section confers no greater entitlement than is available under USERRA.

Employment periods preceding a break in service of more than seven years must be counted in determining whether the employee has been employed for at least 12 months where a written agreement, including a collective bargaining agreement, exists concerning the employer's intention to rehire the employee after the break in service (such as for education or childrearing purposes).

If an employee is maintained on the payroll for any part of a week, including any periods of paid or unpaid leave (such as sick or vacation) during which other benefits or compensation are provided by the employer (such as workers' compensation or group health plan benefits), that entire week counts as a week of employment; for intermittent, occasional, or casual employment, 52 weeks is deemed equal to 12 months.

Employers are permitted to consider an employee's employment prior to a continuous break in service of more than seven years when determining whether the 12-month requirement is met, but if an employer chooses to recognize such prior employment, it must do so uniformly with respect to all employees with similar breaks in service.

Except as provided in paragraph (c)(2) and 29 CFR 825.801 for airline flight crew employees, whether an employee has worked the minimum 1,250 hours of service is determined according to FLSA principles for compensable hours of work (29 CFR part 785); the determining factor is the actual hours worked within the FLSA definition, without limitation by recordkeeping methods or inaccurate compensation agreements, and any accurate accounting of actual hours worked under FLSA principles may be used.

An employee returning from or reemployed following USERRA-covered service must be credited with the hours of service that would have been performed but for the period of absence due to or necessitated by that service, adding them to hours actually worked during the previous 12-month period to satisfy the 1,250-hour requirement; calculations can generally use the employee's pre-service work schedule (subject to 29 CFR 825.801(c) for airline flight crew employees).

If an employer does not maintain an accurate record of hours worked by an employee—including employees exempt from FLSA recordkeeping requirements (such as executive, administrative, and professional employees)—the employer carries the burden of showing that the employee has not worked the required hours (for example, being able to clearly demonstrate that full-time teachers did not work 1,250 hours in the previous 12 months to deny eligibility; subject to 29 CFR 825.801(d) for airline flight crew employees).

The determination of whether an employee meets the hours of service requirement and has at least 12 months of total employment must be made as of the date the FMLA leave is to start; if an employee is on non-FMLA leave when the 12-month eligibility requirement is reached, any portion of the leave taken for an FMLA-qualifying reason after meeting eligibility is FMLA leave (referencing 29 CFR 825.300(b) for eligibility notice content).

Whether 50 employees are employed within 75 miles is determined when the employee gives notice of the need for leave; once determined eligible in response to that notice, eligibility for that specific notice is not affected by subsequent employee count changes regardless of whether leave is continuous, intermittent, or reduced schedule; an employer may not terminate leave that has already started if employee count falls below 50, and must grant FMLA benefits if notice is given when 50 or more employees are employed (e.g., notice in August with 60 employees for leave beginning in December when count is expected to drop to 40).
